clinicalPearls: The defining laboratory feature is a raised GGT cholestasis, in sharp contrast with the low-GGT picture of PFIC1 and PFIC2; it is caused by autosomal recessive ABCB4 mutations encoding MDR3.
MDR3 is the canalicular phosphatidylcholine floppase; its deficiency yields phospholipid-poor bile that cannot buffer the detergent toxicity of bile salts, injuring canaliculi and bile ducts.
Onset is generally later and the severity spectrum broader than PFIC1 or PFIC2, ranging from infancy through childhood to adult presentation.
Cholesterol gallstones and intrahepatic lithiasis are common, and ABCB4 variants underlie the low phospholipid-associated cholelithiasis (LPAC) syndrome.
Histology can mimic large-duct obstruction, with ductular proliferation, portal inflammation, bile duct injury and progressive portal fibrosis.
Related milder phenotypes from ABCB4 variation include intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy and some drug-induced and transient cholestasis.
Ursodeoxycholic acid is often effective, particularly in patients who retain residual MDR3 function.
Untreated disease progresses to biliary cirrhosis and portal hypertension.
reference.pathophysiology: ABCB4 encodes MDR3, an ATP-binding cassette transporter that acts as a floppase translocating phosphatidylcholine across the canalicular membrane into bile. Biliary phospholipids form mixed micelles with bile salts and cholesterol, buffering the detergent toxicity of bile acids and keeping cholesterol in solution. When MDR3 is absent or reduced, bile becomes phospholipid-poor, so free bile salts damage the canalicular membrane and biliary epithelium, generate cholangitis-like bile duct injury and ductular reaction, and promote cholesterol crystallisation and gallstone formation. The resulting cholangiocyte injury explains the elevated GGT that distinguishes this subtype, while the degree of residual transporter activity correlates with later onset, milder disease and responsiveness to ursodeoxycholic acid.
additionalDifferentials: Primary sclerosing cholangitis and autoimmune sclerosing cholangitis
Low phospholipid-associated cholelithiasis (as part of the ABCB4 spectrum)
additionalInvestigations: Serum GGT (raised) with serum bile acids
Liver biopsy showing bile duct injury, ductular reaction and portal fibrosis
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography to exclude mechanical obstruction or sclerosing cholangitis
Abdominal ultrasound for gallstones and intrahepatic lithiasis
Specialist analysis of biliary phospholipid content where available
redFlags: Features of portal hypertension such as varices and splenomegaly
Obstructive jaundice suggesting a stone or stricture
reference.prognosis: The course is variable: ursodeoxycholic acid-responsive disease may remain stable for years, whereas others progress to biliary cirrhosis requiring transplantation. There is an increased burden of cholelithiasis and a recognised risk of biliary malignancy.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosis as primary sclerosing cholangitis or mechanical obstruction, leading to unnecessary surgery
Overlooking ABCB4 disease in adults with idiopathic cholestasis, intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy or recurrent gallstones
Withholding a trial of ursodeoxycholic acid
Assuming all PFIC subtypes share a low GGT
